newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST-November US trade gap seen wider.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-November US trade gap seen wider.

text.p: U.S. import-export data may not have staged another crowd-pleasing performance in November economists said, adding that October's dramatic trade improvement was probably due to one-time factors.

Data on the U.S. trade gap in goods and services is due for release at 0830 EST/1330 on Friday. Forecasters polled by Reuters expect, on average, the trade gap widened to $9.8 billion in November after shrinking 30.2 percent to $7.99 billion in October.

"The special factors we think contributed about $1.0 billion in improvment to the U.S. trade balance last month and that is not going to be repeated again," said John Rothfield, international economist at Nationsbanc-CRT.
A bundling of civilian aircraft exports, which are normally volatile on a month-to-month basis and jumped 130 percent to $1.749 billion in October, may not have recurred in November, analysts said.
In addition, economists said a labor strike by Canadian automotive workers and a surge in Mexican imports took a major slice off the trade number in October.
Moreover, while the U.S. economy shows signs of acceleration in the final quarter of 1996, many of its major trading partners are struggling economically.
So, as robust demand in the U.S. sucks in more imports, weak overseas economies may resist U.S. goods, which are growing costlier as the dollar appreciates, economists said.

"With the combination of three things: slow growth overseas, a strong dollar, then U.S. economic growth picking up steam, I think we will see probably the trade deficit deteriorating," said Sung Won Sohn, chief economist at Norwest Corp.

Rather than standing out as an unusually good number, October's trade deficit probably revived the tendency towards gradually improving trade data, said Josh Feinman, global markets economist at Bankers Trust Co.

"We had some aberrantly bad numbers in the third quarter," Feinman said. "But the underlying trend is probably somewhere in between. November will probably be somewhere in between October and third-quarter numbers."
Exports rose 4.2 percent to a record in October.

But economists said a conservative estimate would have U.S. overseas sales falling about 1.0 percent in November, while imports probably rose 1.5 percent in November, more than reversing a 0.7-percent October fall.
Bilaterally, experts said the alarming gap with Japan, which widened almost 31 percent to $4.958 billion in November, likely narrowed slightly in November.

"October is a month where typically the deficit (with Japan) is the highest of the year," Rothfield of Nationsbanc said. "We think that deficit will fall to $4.5 billion but that is still a disappointing number."
But the dollar may not be overly sensitive to the U.S. trade position with Japan at the moment, analysts said.

A higher-than-forecast trade deficit might temporarily depress the dollar, but Japan's economic problems and the absence of Bank of Japan intervention to weaken the dollar should outweigh potentially bearish trade considerations, economists said.
"There is an asymmetry here in the sense the dollar would benefit more from a good number than it would be hurt by a bad number," Rothfield said.
